newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Christopher presses home Hebron message.
newsitem.headline: Christopher presses home Hebron message.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher kept pressure on Israel on Monday to carry out a long-delayed troop pullback from the West Bank city of Hebron without reopening the deal with the PLO.
"I think we also have an acute sense of the shortness of time and desire that we make progress as rapidly as possible," he told reporters after meeting Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy.

Israeli and Palestinian negotiatiators were due to reconvene later in the day in Gaza to discuss the Hebron issue after a U.S.-mediated meeting on Sunday set a framework for intensive talks on the problem.
The talks, shrouded in a news blackout, are due to centre on Hebron and economic matters on Mondays and Wednesdays and on security and Palestinian civilian arrangements on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

Christopher, ending a two-day visit to Israel and Gaza, said pointedly that he was reassured that "Israel does not intend to try to rescind or modify" existing accords "but only to implement them in an effective and practical way".

Israel and the PLO, moving back from the brink, agreed at Sunday's three-hour meeting at the Erez crossing in Gaza to hold intensive talks on how to proceed with the long-delayed partial pullout from Hebron, home to 100,000 Arabs.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said clashes, in which 59 Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed -- an Arab policeman died of his wounds on Monday -- made ensuring security for 400 Jewish settlers in Hebron even more imperative.
Christopher said Israel and the PLO would have to take account their recent wave of bloodshed in deciding how to carry out the redeployment.
"Now within the implementation, practical questions arise and I think it's only fair to say that those practical questions now involve the recent violence," Christopher said.

Christopher was sent to the area after U.S. President Bill Clinton held an Arab-Israeli summit in Washington to end the clashes triggered by Israel's opening of an archaelogical tourist tunnel near Moslem holy places in Jerusalem.
In another sign of an easing of tensions, Israeli President Ezer Weizman invited Arafat to visit his home in the seaside town of Caesarea on Tuesday.
Arafat has visited Israeli publicly once before, when he paid a condolence call on the widow of assassinated Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin last November in Tel Aviv.
Israeli and Palestinian negotiators were expected to focus their discussions on Monday on finding a venue where they could hold non-stop talks on Hebron.

Palestinian officials said the PLO wanted the negotiations to be held in the Egyptian Red Sea resort of Taba, the scene of previous self-rule talks. Israeli officials said they preferred staying in Erez.
Israeli-Egyptian relations have been strained since the election of the right-wing Netanyahu in May. Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak stayed away from last week's Washington summit.
Levy said the talks should be held alternately at an Israeli location and a Palestinian one, reflecting Israel's demand for "reciprocity" in any deal forged with the PLO. .
But Levy and Christopher said they didn't believe the venue had to be a problem.
"The consideration is to move to a venue where the discussions can be more continuous than they are under the present circumstances," Christopher said.
